explain.say: Construction is one of the most dangerous jobs in the world. In the United States, falls alone cause roughly a third of construction worker deaths. Yet most accidents are foreseeable, and engineers can design many of them away. The key tool is this ladder of choices, the hierarchy of controls, best at the top.

explain.say: Start at the top. The best control eliminates the hazard: assemble a roof truss on the ground and lift it, so nobody works at height. Next, substitute something safer. Then engineering controls like guardrails and trench boxes, then rules and training. Personal protective equipment, the hard hat and harness, is the last line. Why is PPE the weakest?

explain.say: Because it only works if worn right, every time! Safety agencies talk of a fatal four, the hazards behind most site deaths: falls, being struck by something, electrocution, and being caught in or between things, like a collapsing trench. Look at the groups. Which have you seen near a building site?

draw.question: OSHA's fatal four: which hazard is it?

explain.say: Ladders cause many falls, so remember the one in four rule. For every four metres up, the foot goes one metre out, an angle of about seventy five degrees. A ladder reaching six metres up the wall needs its foot one and a half metres out, and should stick up about a metre above the landing to hold on to.

explain.say: Before work starts, each hazard is scored: likelihood times severity, each one to five. A fall from a roof edge, likely four, severe five, scores twenty, so it is tackled first. Trenches over about one point two metres deep need support or battering back. Superb! Challenge: how far out should the foot of a ladder be to reach eight metres?

faq.q: What is the hierarchy of controls?
faq.a: An order for managing hazards: eliminate, substitute, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment last. Higher controls protect everyone without relying on behaviour.
asks: What is the hierarchy of controls in construction?

faq.q: What are the fatal four in construction?
faq.a: The US safety agency OSHA's term for the leading causes of construction deaths: falls, struck-by incidents, electrocution, and caught-in or caught-between incidents.
asks: What are the fatal four hazards?

faq.q: What is the ladder 4 to 1 rule?
faq.a: Set a leaning ladder one unit out from the wall for every four units up, about 75 degrees. A ladder reaching 6 metres up needs its foot 1.5 metres out.
asks: What angle should a ladder be at?

faq.q: How is a risk assessment scored?
faq.a: Each hazard gets a likelihood score and a severity score, often 1 to 5, and they are multiplied. High scores, like 20 for a fall from a roof edge, need action first.

faq.q: When does a trench need support?
faq.a: UK guidance treats trenches deeper than about 1.2 metres as needing support or sloping sides; US rules require a protective system from 1.5 metres. Any trench can collapse, so check every one.

facts: OSHA's fatal four are falls, struck-by, electrocution and caught-in or between.
The 1 in 4 rule puts a ladder at about 75° to the ground.
